key_insight: Machine-learned nanosecond dynamics show that oxygen-vacancy–reduced rutile TiO2(110) has drastically suppressed small-polaron mobility because surface hopping pathways are strongly constrained.
engineering_relevance: This explains why porous rutile TiO2 can exhibit much lower electron mobility than single-crystal material, informing the design of oxide surfaces for catalysis, photovoltaics, and energy storage.
method: Extended machine-learning-assisted polaron dynamics from bulk oxides to a redox-active surface.
Ran several nanoseconds of finite-temperature dynamics on oxygen-deficient rutile TiO2(110).
Compared surface and bulk hopping pathways to map the polaron free-energy landscape.
evidence_signal: Nanosecond-scale simulations over a range of temperatures revealed that surface polaron mobility is orders of magnitude lower than in bulk, with hopping mostly confined to planar inter-row trajectories and only rare interlayer events.
watch_item: The result is specific to a model oxide surface and depends on the quality and transferability of the machine-learning dynamics model to other reducible oxides and defect configurations.
paper_title: Machine-learned dynamics of surface polarons at reduced oxide surfaces
